note.text: Logic studies how reasons support conclusions. An argument is not merely a quarrel: it contains claims offered as reasons and a claim those reasons are meant to support. Reasons are premises; the claim supported is the conclusion. An inference is the step from premises to conclusion. First identify what a speaker is trying to establish, then ask whether the reasons actually support it. A confident voice, popularity or repetition does not establish that an inference is good.

sections.heading: Understand the ideas
sections.text: Logic studies how reasons support conclusions. An argument is not merely a quarrel: it contains claims offered as reasons and a claim those reasons are meant to support. Reasons are premises; the claim supported is the conclusion. An inference is the step from premises to conclusion. First identify what a speaker is trying to establish, then ask whether the reasons actually support it. A confident voice, popularity or repetition does not establish that an inference is good.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: At a Bamenda school, Bih argues that the library should open after lessons because pupils need a quiet place to read. The proposed opening is the conclusion; the need for quiet reading space is a reason. Another pupil might agree with the conclusion while questioning whether staffing makes the plan possible. Separate the proposal from its support before judging it.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Underline a proposed conclusion and list the reasons separately. Words such as because and therefore may help, but they are clues rather than guarantees. Ask whether a sentence is giving support or receiving support. A collection of unrelated statements is not automatically an argument.
